extracted.intended_audience: aspiring op-ed and column writers (journalists, academics, policy professionals, students)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing short opinion pieces (op-eds or columns) that present a focused point of view, grounded in research, and aimed at a targeted readership; covers structure (opening, topic/theme, ending), voice, research, and revision checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length / Conciseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically, it is short, between 750 and 800 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Op-eds/columns should be brief and tightly written; adhere to roughly 750–800 words to fit common publication formats and to maintain focus and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly defined point
rubrics_metrics.description: It has a clearly defined point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before writing ask: Do I have a clear point to make? What is it? The central point should be explicit and drive the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly defined point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: It has a clearly defined point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State an identifiable perspective or stance and ensure the column consistently reflects that POV throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: It represents clarity of thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece should demonstrate logical progression and lucid argumentation; use the revision checklist (check clarity) to ensure ideas are clearly expressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong, unique voice
rubrics_metrics.description: It contains the strong, unique voice of the writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a distinctive voice appropriate to the piece and audience. Voice can be conversational, contemplative, humorous, authoritative, etc. Practice by reading the piece out loud to judge voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience targeting ('Who cares?')
rubrics_metrics.description: Write with a particular audience in mind; identify who you are trying to convince and why you are targeting that reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask 'Who cares?' to shape tone, examples, and level of explanation — tailoring the piece to the intended readership improves persuasiveness and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance to the argument / Research grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Columns and op-ed pieces must be grounded in solid research: facts, quotations, citations, data, or personal observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research strengthens opinion pieces and can include sensory detail. Two basic research methods: field research (scene visits, interviews, primary materials) and library/academic/internet research (secondary materials, graphs, charts, scholarly articles). Use reliable sources to back claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic (definition and placement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Topic: the person, place, issue, incident, or thing that is the primary focus of the column; the topic is usually stated in the first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly identify the central subject early (often first paragraph) so readers immediately know what the piece is about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme (overarching idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theme: another level of meaning to the topic — the big, overarching idea or point of importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide what broader idea your topic illustrates; the theme may appear early or later and can serve as a turning point into deeper argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening / First-line hook
rubrics_metrics.description: The first line of an op-ed is crucial; the opening 'hook' may grab the reader with a strong claim, a surprising fact, a metaphor, a mystery, or a counter-intuitive observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the opening to entice the reader and to briefly lay the foundation for your argument. Choose a hook type that best serves your theme and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ending requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Every good column or op-ed needs a strong ending which: echoes or answers the introduction; has been foreshadowed by preceding thematic statements; contains a final epiphany or calls the reader to action; is the last and often most memorable detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for an ending that resolves or crystallizes your point and leaves a lasting impression; ensure the conclusion has been set up by the body of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ending type: open vs closed
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two basic types of endings: an 'open ending' suggests rather than states a conclusion, while a 'closed ending' states rather than suggests a conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closed endings, where the point is resolved, are by far the most commonly used in op-eds; choose the type that fits your rhetorical goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice and tone (style range and conventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Columns are most typically conversational in tone, but voice can range widely (contemplative, descriptive, informative, humorous, reportorial, self-effacing, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the publication and audience guide voice; reading the piece aloud helps you assess how the voice will come across. Match tone to purpose — conversational for accessibility, authoritative for expertise, humorous for levity, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision — Check clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Check clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During revision, ensure sentences and argumentation are clear and unambiguous; remove clutter and clarify any vague claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision — Check coherence and unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Check coherence and unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure paragraphs and transitions form a unified argument that consistently supports the main point; delete or revise tangents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision — Check simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Check simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple, direct phrasing over jargon or convoluted constructions to make the piece accessible and punchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision — Check voice and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Check voice and tone. (Most are conversational; some require an authoritative voice.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure tone is consistent and appropriate for the intended reader and publication; adapt if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision — Verify quotations and paraphrasing accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Check direct quotations and paraphrasing for accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm that quotes are exact and paraphrases accurately reflect the source; inaccuracies undermine credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision — Credit sources appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Check to make sure you properly credit all sources (though formal citations are not necessary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient attribution (named sources, data provenance) to support claims without requiring academic citation format unless requested by the outlet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision — Consistency of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Check the consistency of your opinion throughout your op-ed or column.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure your stated stance does not contradict earlier claims and that supporting points all reinforce the central argument.
